claims.text: The applicable starting material is a single-phase solid-solution high-entropy alloy in which titanium and nickel are primary constituents.
A minor zirconium addition can act as an oxygen and nitrogen getter in the titanium-nickel-based alloy.
Trace oxygen and nitrogen promote phase segregation during thermal aging.
Interstitial oxygen and nitrogen initially contribute to solid-solution strengthening.
Thermal-aging-induced depletion of interstitial solutes from the metal matrix causes progressive softening.
Reducing oxygen and nitrogen incorporation will suppress secondary-phase formation or precipitation.
Secondary-phase formation or precipitation undermines solid-solution strengthening.
Zirconium preferentially reacts with residual oxygen and nitrogen to form stable oxides or nitrides.
The zirconium-derived oxides or nitrides will form outside the primary alloy matrix.
Getter addition will prevent depletion of strengthening interstitials from the alloy matrix.
Getter addition will delay or prevent phase segregation during high-temperature exposure.
The getter-enhanced alloy will retain higher strength than the getter-free control after prolonged high-temperature exposure.
The getter-enhanced alloy will exhibit less high-temperature softening than the getter-free control.
A getter-free titanium-nickel-based alloy is expected to undergo impurity-induced phase segregation and softening near 700°C.
A TiVNbTa refractory high-entropy alloy undergoes microstructural evolution and mechanical softening upon aging at 700°C.
The hypothesis is intended to apply around 700°C when trace oxygen and nitrogen are present.
The TiVNbTa impurity mechanism may not transfer directly to titanium-nickel-based high-entropy alloys.

contradictions.description: The structural mediator proposes reducing oxygen and nitrogen in the matrix, while the mechanism says getter scavenging prevents depletion of strengthening interstitials. Scavenging oxygen and nitrogen from the matrix would itself tend to deplete those interstitials, so the proposed direction of interstitial control is internally inconsistent.

The hypothesis frames oxygen and nitrogen primarily as harmful impurities to be removed, whereas the mechanism also identifies them as strengthening solutes whose depletion causes softening. It does not explain how zirconium selectively removes the segregation-driving fraction without eliminating the strengthening fraction.
